articleTitle: The use of formal methods in communications standards
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Formal Methods for Protocols
abstract: Formal (i.e. mathematical) methods in computer science have been under development for the past 50 years, but the last 15 years has seen a great surge of interest in formal methods for specification. Communication systems have been a popular area for application of formal methods as they exhibit challenging technical features such as concurrency and distribution. The trend towards open systems, such as found in the ISO work on OSI) open systems interconnection), has provided a strong impetus for methods that allow interfaces and services to be specified precisely. In recognition of this, CCITT began work in 1976 on standardising SDL (specification and description language, Z.100) as a formal notation for telecommunications systems. Similarly ISO began work in 1980 on standardising Estelle (Extended finite state machine language, ISO 9074) and LOTOS (Language Of Temporal Ordering Specification, ISO 8807) for formal specification of open systems standards. All three languages reached a stable state in 1988, and have been widely applied to specifying communications standards.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Formal design techniques in the implementation of concurrency
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Formal Methods for Protocols
abstract: Describes the design of the INMOS H-1 processor. This is a high performance implementation of the transputer currently under design. The H-1 will support a full implementation of OCCAM where communication with other processors is achieved by multiplexing messages from 'virtual channels' down the physical link channels. Such multiplexing is achieved through packetising the message and adding header information to indicate the ultimate destination of the packet. These packets are routed through a network by routing switches. Each packet is transmitted as a sequence of bytes with each byte being handshaken. On top of this byte level protocol is a packet level protocol which handshakes each packet across the network.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Formal Methods for Protocols
abstract: This paper discusses existing practice for OSI protocol development and then introduces new technologies utilising the formal description technique LOTOS. Particular emphasis is placed on the industrial applicability of the techniques described based on current experience with British Telecom. Many of the results described are being developed through collaborative projects with European initiatives such as Esprit II and RACE. The current focus for this work is the Esprit LOTOSPHERE project which is developing technologies to exploit LOTOS covering the complete protocol development lifecycle.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: CCS-recent applications, experience with tools, current and planned research
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Formal Methods for Protocols
abstract: The Mathematically Proven Safety Systems (MPSS) project in the Laboratory for Foundations of Computer Science of Edinburgh University is applying state-of the-art formal reasoning techniques and tools to the design of safety critical system. During the first year of the project the author has concentrated on process calculi and model-based approaches. One major case study concerned with reactor protection has been completed. This is the primary subject of this paper. On-going work includes investigations into the hazard analysis process and how formal descriptions of safety properties can be generated from this process. These properties would then be carried forward as proof obligations in the actual system design stage. Further case study work in progress includes several examples in railway signalling. All of the case studies so far conducted have static safe states (e.g. signals set to red, control rods in).<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
